newsitem.title: JAPAN: Okinawa governor gives green light on U.S. bases.
newsitem.headline: Okinawa governor gives green light on U.S. bases.

text.p: Okinawa Governor Masahide Ota said on Friday he would take steps to renew leases for U.S. military bases on the island, ending a bitter standoff with the central government.
Analysts said the governor's decision could affect Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto's political schedule, including the timing of general elections.
"This is the most difficult decision I, as the head of the administration, have made in the past six years," Ota told a televised news conference in Naha, the Okinawa prefectural capital.
Officials said Ota would soon start the legal process allowing the leases to be extended.

Following the rape last year of an Okinawan schoolgirl by three U.S. servicemen, a case that re-ignited protests against the presence of the U.S. military on the island, Ota refused to sign orders to renew leases for the facilities.

Ota's decision comes three days after he won a promise from Hashimoto that Okinawa would get special funds to improve the economy of the prefecture, the poorest in Japan with average income half the level of Tokyo's.

Hashimoto pledged renewed efforts this week to reduce the bases and set up a five billion yen ($45.8 million) fund for the economic development of Okinawa if Ota would ease calls for a total pullout of U.S. forces, which are seen by Tokyo as a bulwark of regional security.
The leases, held by some 3,000 landowners opposed to U.S. military bases, expire next May, which made Ota's refusal a potential threat to U.S. use of the facilities.

The subtropical island, some 1,000 km (625 miles) southwest of Tokyo, is home to three-quarters of the U.S. military facilities in Japan and about half of the 47,000 U.S. military personnel stationed in the country, although it constitutes less than one percent of Japan's total land area.
Okinawans have long complained about the heavy concentration of U.S. bases on the island.
In a visit to Tokyo in April, U.S. President Bill Clinton announced base consolidations on the island that cut the area they occupy by about by about 20 percent.
In a referendum last Sunday, Okinawans voted overwhelmingly to call for a reduction in the U.S. military presence and Ota wants all the bases closed by 2015.

Late last month, the 15-member Grand Bench of Japan's Supreme Court ruled unanimously that Okinawa must appropriate land for U.S. military bases, rejecting an appeal by Ota that the military presence was unconstitutional.
Most of the land for the 40 odd bases on Okinawa was first appropriated between the end of World War Two and 1972, when Okinawa was under U.S. military rule.
Hashimoto, who took office in January, has said he will give top priority to reducing the heavy concentration of U.S. military bases on the island.
He has said his decision on whether and when to call a general election would depend on developments over Okinawa and the latest state of economy.

"It is not appropriate to talk about the dissolution of the Lower House (for general elections) without resolving the Okinawa issue," top government spokesman Seiroku Kajiyama told Friday's cabinet meeting.
Hashimoto need not call an election until next July.
Japanese media, some politicians and analysts have predicted that Hashimoto will hold elections for the powerful 500-seat Lower House of parliament on October 20.
